text: Sudden, unexplained cattle death (found simply dead, or dying within ~24 hours with vague signs, or within a few hours with identifiable signs) can rarely be treated in time, but correct diagnosis matters a lot for protecting other in-contact cattle. Anthrax: caused by the bacterium Bacillus Anthracis, picked up from soil, and can also infect humans by contact, inhalation, or ingestion. Cattle are often simply found dead, sometimes with dark bloody discharge from the mouth/anus and rapid body decomposition after death; less acute cases show great weakness, fever up to 41.5°C, breathing difficulty, blood in urine/milk/feces, and incoordination/convulsions. Do NOT open the carcass — exposed blood spreads spores into the soil that survive for years, and most outbreaks actually happen in areas with a past Anthrax death. Treatment (penicillin or tetracycline) only helps if given very early, before symptoms are obvious — once seen, it's usually too late. Prevention: vaccination is effective but takes 10–14 days for full immunity; at-risk cattle (e.g. grazing where an animal recently died of Anthrax) should get immediate long-acting antibiotic to stop any incubating infection, with vaccination following about 7–10 days later (never combine antibiotics and vaccination at the same time). Blackleg: caused by the bacterium Clostridium Chauvei, not spread animal-to-animal — picked up by grazing short grass contaminated with soil-surviving spores, especially after heavy rain. Mainly affects young animals (6–24 months) in good condition; death is sudden (12–48 hours), often with the animal simply found dead. Less acute signs: severe lameness, and characteristic hot, painful, crepitant (crackling on touch) swelling in the hip, neck, or shoulder muscle that enlarges rapidly as the skin above it turns cold and numb; affected muscle at necropsy is dark red-to-black and spongy. Treatment: only effective very early, at the lameness/hot-swelling stage, with a high dose of penicillin/amoxicillin. Prevention: vaccination is effective (often a '7-way' Clostridium vaccine covering Blackleg, Tetanus, Botulism, etc.); at-risk cattle (grazing where an animal previously died of Blackleg) should get immediate long-acting amoxicillin, with vaccination 7–10 days later.
